prize_parts.citation: for theories of firm heterogeneity and selection showing how exporting, foreign investment and reallocation across firms shape the gains from trade

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: B044, with Melitz and Helpman. The reasons are the same, and the exchange tested them rather than replacing them. Melitz (2003) is a single originating model. It moved the unit of analysis in trade from the industry to the firm and made selection, within-industry reallocation and the extensive margin central to who gains from trade. Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exporting versus foreign direct investment is a separable and natural complement. The mechanism has had more than twenty years to be confronted with firm-level data from many countries, and the disputes concern the size of welfare gains, not whether selection and reallocation exist. It is a later and distinct advance on the increasing-returns theory recognised in 2008. After reading round 1, I give less weight to adjacency to earlier prizes than I did, and I now treat it as a timing consideration and not a scientific objection. Dreber and Hjalmarsson both make this point persuasively. What keeps B044 first is the combination of a clear conceptual break, long confirmation and a credit boundary I can draw with reasonable confidence. That boundary is imperfect, and I say so below. I do not rest the case on the 5-4-2 split in round 1. That split is a count of preferences, not evidence, and it is below six votes.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still attribution. Bernard and Jensen documented the exporter facts that motivated the theory. Eaton and Kortum built a related quantitative strand. None of them is on the B044 ballot, and the ballot's credited names are only Helpman, Melitz and Redding. A two-name award therefore leaves parts of the field's origin story uncredited, and I cannot widen the group to include them within the shortlisted names. Redding is on the ballot, but I regard his strongest contributions as later quantitative and spatial extensions. Welfare magnitudes depend on Pareto productivity and CES demand, so the citation should name the mechanism and not the magnitudes. Trade was recognised in 2008, and some members may weigh that for field balance, though I do not think it should decide the question. B038 has the more direct bearing on current debates about technology and globalisation, and several colleagues find its empirical designs more transparent than the structural trade literature. That is a serious rival on importance. My difference with its supporters is about credit boundaries, not about merit.

responses.point: Dreber argues that adjacency to the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes should count against B038 only if an earlier citation covered the same discovery. She says it did not, and she reads my ranking of B044 above B038 as a difference of weighting, not of merit.
responses.response: I accept this standard and I have changed my reasoning because of it. In round 1 I leaned on the Acemoglu and Card overlaps more than the written citations justify. Card (2021) and Acemoglu (2024) did not cover technology and trade exposure in local labour markets, and Goldin (2023) did not cover wage-structure evidence. I should apply the same standard to B044, where the 2008 citation covered earlier scale-based trade theory and not firm selection. I therefore no longer count either prize as a point against its candidate. What remains between B044 and B038 is attribution, namely whether there is one discovery with a defensible boundary. You are right that this is a difference of weighting and not a verdict on merit.

responses.point: Boppart reads the skill-demand and trade-shock strands as one question about how technology and trade shift labour demand. He holds that Autor, Hanson and Katz cover both strands within the cap, and he accepts that Dorn would displace Katz if the strands are split. He ranks B044 second and calls the Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum gap its main weakness.
responses.response: His own conditional answers the question I raised in round 1. The case for a three-name B038 award depends on treating the strands as one discovery, and he says honestly that he holds this with uncertainty. I find the unity argument more credible than I did, because Autor's work spans both strands and Katz is the benchmark for the wage-structure question. It still leaves the Dorn-versus-Katz choice to a judgement that neither of us can settle from this evidence. I agree with him that the empirical foundations of B044 sit outside the two names. The difference is that the B044 gap concerns who else deserves credit in a field, whereas the B038 gap also concerns where the discovery's own boundary lies. I put the second as the weightier problem, but the margin is small and I treat B038 as my first alternative.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson would define the B044 award as the integrated theoretical framework of selection and reallocation, not the whole firm-level trade agenda. She separates the well-confirmed qualitative mechanism from the model-dependent welfare magnitudes, and she would support B038 if the committee found a way to credit Dorn.
responses.response: I can accept a citation worded that way without reducing the claim, and it is the answer I would give to the chair's question. I would exclude Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum from this award because the prize rewards the general-equilibrium model that made selection a mechanism, not the discovery of exporter heterogeneity as a stylised fact. The facts motivated the theory but did not provide the framework. Eaton-Kortum is a different, Ricardian strand and does not substitute for the selection mechanism. I would not claim the boundary is undisputed. A two-name award leaves out real contributors, and the committee should state that openly. The citation I now propose therefore names exporting, foreign investment and reallocation, and it makes no claim about welfare magnitudes. Your remark on Dorn is the same boundary problem on the other side of the table.

responses.point: Friberg argues that a prize is not a quota for a field and that trade has had no recognition since 2008. He says Eaton-Kortum is a different strand from Melitz, so it weakens the case for widening the group. He accepts that some empirical credit cannot be recognised in a two-name award.
responses.response: I agree on both points, and the first one helps me. Because I should not treat the 2008 prize as a quota, I discard it as an argument for B044 as well as against it. The question is only whether the advance is separable and mature, and I think it is. I also accept your distinction between the Ricardian strand and the selection mechanism. The Bernard-Jensen empirical work is the harder gap, and I share your view that it has to be handled by wording the citation around the theory. I would add one caveat to your cap argument. The three-person cap would allow Redding as a third name, but I would still leave him out, because adding an extender would blur an attribution that is otherwise unusually clean.

responses.point: Fredriksson treats the technology and trade strands as one programme with a shared question and Autor as the common thread. He calls Dorn versus Hanson the hardest call within B038, and he describes a trade-shock-only award as a fallback he would weigh. He counts neighbouring prizes as a modest timing consideration.
responses.response: I agree with his timing point, and I take his statement that the case rests on treating the two strands as one discovery at face value. That is also what I would need to see resolved before B038 became my preferred part. First, I would want the committee to say whether the discovery is the determinants of labour demand or the adjustment to trade shocks, because the answer decides between Katz and Dorn. Second, I would want a citation that names the empirical contribution and not the whole task framework, so that the Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane gap is stated, not hidden. I cannot assess shift-share persistence independently. I note that it concerns the same kind of local-adjustment question that economic historians study for railways and electrification. I regard it as a question about wording and timing more than about whether the finding is real. If B044 cannot reach six votes, I would accept B038 with Autor, Hanson and Katz.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum as co-originators whose omission makes a two-name award indefensible. I think a theory-focused citation answers this, but it is a judgement.
Whether Redding should be added. I think not, but the cap would allow it and I cannot rule out that colleagues will see his quantitative work as part of one achievement.
Whether B038 is one discovery or two, and whether the third name should be Katz or Dorn. This is the main thing that could move me to B038 as a preferred part.
How much the model-dependence of gains-from-trade magnitudes (Pareto productivity, CES demand) should count against B044 beyond the wording of the citation.

My assessment relies on my own knowledge of the literatures and on colleagues' statements. I have not independently verified citation, impact or priority claims, and I have not checked the 2008, 2021, 2022, 2023 or 2024 citations against the shortlist.
statement.conflict_note: No documented connection between me and any credited name on B044, B038 or B019 appears in the supplied profile. I disclose field proximity. My research on local effects of railways and electrification, on electricity and labour conflict, and on historical national accounts and regional inequality is close in method to the local labour-market evidence in B038 and to the long-run data in B019. I treat that as a reason for caution and not as evidence of merit. I am a Lund colleague of Tommy Andersson, and I have cross-disciplinary ties to political scientists, none of which bears on the credited names. No recusal is apparent, and conflicts are disclosed but not adjudicated.
